label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $50/MWh on every shocked day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50), which is the dominant loss to the N.Y.C. retail short P5. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A sustained late-June heat dome covers the Lower Hudson Valley and N.Y.C. for 30 days. Transmission limits into the pocket bind on most afternoons, and N.Y.C. on-peak prices separate from WEST by a pocket_minus_ref_usd widening of +90 $/MWh on every day. Load runs 3% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03), which lifts the N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 that is short 140 MW. WEST on-peak, dart, gas and basis are held at neutral so that the loss comes from the congestion channel alone. The +90 $/MWh spread is inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7 $/MWh. Loss is driven by P5 (short N.Y.C.) and only partly offset by P2 (long spread).

A short, intense heat dome lasts 12 days and drives a severe, short-lived N.Y.C. congestion event. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by +200 $/MWh, which is a stress beyond the summer historical maximum of 289.7 but below the implausible ceiling of 363.1. Load runs 10% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.10), which raises the retail load that P5 must serve and increases the size of its spread exposure. WEST on-peak, gas, dart and basis are held neutral so that the scenario isolates the pocket spread and load interaction. The loss is concentrated in the 12-day window rather than spread across the full horizon.

A 30-day heat wave strains the Z6 New York gas delivery market, so N.Y.C. gas costs rise sharply above Henry Hub with an ny_gas_basis_usd of +10 $/MMBtu. Because P4 is a heat-rate call struck on WEST minus 8 times gas, this basis raises its effective strike and cuts the payoff, without moving power prices. Separately, the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by +50 $/MWh for the full period, which hurts the short N.Y.C. retail position P5. Load runs 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05). Gas_hh and WEST on-peak are neutral so that the loss uses the basis channel and congestion channel together. P4 loss is capped at its base payoff, which this scenario does not exhaust.

Load runs at a normal-to-slightly-high 1.0 times typical, so the loss comes from the congestion channel rather than from load. P5 is short 140 MW in N.Y.C. and loses on every day the spread stays wide, while P2 gains only a fraction of that offset. Gas, DART and NY gas basis are held neutral to isolate the spread channel. The shock is within the summer historical range of pocket_minus_ref_usd (hist_max 289.7) and below the implausible ceiling of 363.1.

A 30-day heat wave tightens the Z6 New York gas market so that the N.Y.C. gas cost sits about 20 $/MMBtu above the reference, through ny_gas_basis_usd of +20. This raises the effective strike of the heat-rate call P4 on 50 MW and cuts its payoff, without moving WEST or N.Y.C. power prices. The same heat keeps the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread wider by +50 $/MWh over the full period, which hurts the short N.Y.C. retail position P5. Load runs 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05) as cooling demand builds. WEST on-peak, gas_hh and DART stay neutral so the loss is attributable to the gas-basis channel and the congestion channel together.

A concentrated 14-day heat dome produces a severe N.Y.C. congestion episode. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by +150 $/MWh for the full window, a level below the summer historical maximum of 289.7 $/MWh. Load runs 8% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.08), which adds retail load that P5 must serve at the high spread. WEST on-peak, gas, DART and NY gas basis are neutral so the scenario isolates the pocket spread and load interaction over a shorter, sharper window than the 20-day case. P2 offsets part of the loss through its long spread position, and P1 and P4 are unaffected because WEST prices do not move.

TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: gas_supply
Season: winter


INPUTS

{
 "active_positions": [
  "P1",
  "P2",
  "P3",
  "P4",
  "P5",
  "P6"
 ],
 "allocated_capital_usd": 20000000.0,
 "book": [
  {
   "channel": "system",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price is above K1",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",
   "position": "P1",
   "what": "Long 100 MW swap on the WEST on-peak price, strike K1 = 39.49 $/MWh, 16 h per on-peak weekday"
  },
  {
   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",
   "what": "Retail load obligation: short 140 MW x (load / normal load) in N.Y.C. at fixed price R = 45.65, hedged by a long WEST position at H = 34.05, 24 h; P&L = (R - N.Y.C. price) + (WEST price - H), times load"
  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A four-day gas-supply event tightens delivery into N.Y.C. (Zone J) while upstate gas and hydro remain adequate, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 420 $/MWh on the shocked days. Pocket generators set the marginal price, and WEST on-peak prices barely move. Henry Hub rises 25% as a regional pipeline constraint raises the cost of gas delivered to the city. The Z6 NY gas basis adds 4 $/MWh to the gas cost used by the heat-rate call P4, which lowers its payoff modestly. Load runs 10% above a typical winter day, which increases the size of the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5. The loss is dominated by P5 on the wide pocket spread, partly offset by the long N.Y.C.-WEST spread position P2. The shock is sized near the top of the pocket-minus-reference historical range.

A cold-driven gas delivery shortfall lasts seven days and pushes winter load 20% above a typical day as heating demand peaks. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 220 $/MWh over the period because the city's gas-fired fleet is constrained while upstate supply is adequate. Henry Hub rises 10% and the Z6 NY gas basis adds 1 $/MWh, a small effect that mainly lowers P4. Real-time prices clear 40% below day-ahead as the forecast overstates the peak, which hurts the long real-time position in P1 and P3's dart exposure. The short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 is the main driver of loss, with the load ratio amplifying its cost on each day. The long N.Y.C.-WEST spread P2 offsets part of the loss. This scenario tests the combination of a sustained high load and a moderate spread, with the load channel dominant.

A gas delivery constraint into N.Y.C. persists for twenty-five days with a modest daily effect. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 70 $/MWh each day, a level that is well inside the historical range but is sustained across the month. Henry Hub rises 10% over the period as storage drawdowns tighten the regional market, which raises WEST on-peak prices slightly and supports the long WEST swap P1. Load stays at its typical winter level, so the loss comes from the persistence of the spread rather than from load. The short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 accumulates a steady loss across many days, partly offset by the long N.Y.C.-WEST spread P2 and the modest gain in P1. The scenario tests the book's exposure to a long, shallow spread widening rather than a short spike.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A three-day N.Y.C. gas delivery squeeze coincides with a sharp cold-driven load peak. Gas-fired pocket units cannot obtain firm supply, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread widens by 340 $/MWh on each shocked day, close to the Winter Storm Elliott spread. Load runs 15% above a typical winter day, which enlarges the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 on every hour it serves. Henry Hub rises 30% on the shocked days and the Z6 NY gas basis adds 3 $/MWh, which lowers the heat-rate call P4. WEST prices are held at their unshocked level, so the long WEST swap P1 and the WEST-referenced positions do not move. The short, intense spread event tests the book's largest single-day exposure, with P5 carrying nearly all of the loss and P2 offsetting only a small part.

A ten-day gas supply tightness into N.Y.C. keeps the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread wide at 300 $/MWh on every shocked day. Scarce pocket gas forces the city to rely on expensive real-time balancing, so real-time on-peak prices clear 60% above day-ahead, which hurts the day-ahead-minus-real-time receipt in P3. Henry Hub rises 20% and the Z6 NY gas basis adds 2 $/MWh, a modest move that mainly lowers the heat-rate call P4. Load runs 10% above a typical winter day, increasing the size of the short retail obligation P5. The loss accumulates over the full ten days, so duration matters as well as magnitude, and the long WEST swap P1 gains only slightly from the higher gas-linked WEST price. This scenario combines a persistent pocket spread with a real-time premium, a channel not used in the earlier scenarios.

A five-day cold snap tightens gas delivery into the city without moving Henry Hub, so the gas shock is purely local. Winter load runs 25% above a typical day as heating demand peaks, which is at the high end of the historical load ratio and well inside the implausibility ceiling. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 250 $/MWh because the city's gas-fired fleet is constrained while upstate supply remains adequate. Real-time prices clear 80% above day-ahead as the city balances the system in real time, which reduces P3's receipt and adds to the loss. The short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 is the dominant loss, scaled up by the high load ratio on every hour. The long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 are essentially unaffected because WEST prices and gas do not move.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Winter load runs 25% above a typical day as heating demand peaks, which enlarges the short retail obligation P5 on every hour it serves. Henry Hub is unchanged, so the shock is a purely local supply constraint rather than a national gas price move. WEST prices are held at their unshocked level, so the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 are essentially flat. The loss is driven by the accumulated spread over eight days and the elevated load, with the long N.Y.C.-WEST spread P2 offsetting only part of it. This tests a longer, moderate-intensity pocket squeeze with a load channel, distinct from the short intense events already run.

A continental gas price surge lifts Henry Hub 80% over six days as storage drawdowns and pipeline outages hit the national market. The Z6 NY gas basis widens by 10 $/MWh, which raises the effective gas cost used by the heat-rate call P4 and lowers its payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 260 $/MWh because gas-fired pocket units set the marginal price in the city while upstate hydro and nuclear limit the WEST move. Winter load runs 10% above a typical day. WEST on-peak prices are not moved separately, so the long WEST swap P1 gains little. The loss accumulates across the six days, dominated by the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 and the gas-linked loss on P4, with P2 offsetting part of the spread loss. The scenario tests a broad gas-price shock combined with a sustained pocket spread.

A four-day intense gas shortage in N.Y.C. widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread by 380 $/MWh on each shocked day, close to the Winter Storm Elliott pocket spread of 338.5 $/MWh. Henry Hub rises 15% and the Z6 NY gas basis adds 2 $/MWh, which lowers the heat-rate call P4 modestly. Winter load runs 20% above a typical day, enlarging the short retail obligation P5. The loss is dominated by P5 on the wide spread and the real-time premium, with P2 offsetting part of the spread. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Henry Hub is unchanged, but a local pipeline and compressor failure into the city raises the Z6 NY delivered gas basis by 15 $/MWh over six days. The N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread widens by 240 $/MWh because pocket units cannot buy gas at the hub price and set the city's marginal price. Winter load runs 10% above a typical day, which enlarges the short retail obligation P5. The 15 $/MWh basis is added to the gas cost used by the heat-rate call P4, lowering its payoff, while WEST prices and Henry Hub are held fixed so the long WEST swap P1 is flat. The loss is dominated by P5 on the wide spread, with the P4 basis hit as a secondary channel and P2 offsetting part of the spread. This tests a basis-only gas shock that leaves the national gas price unmoved.

A cold-season gas tightness lasts eighteen days, the longest duration in this set, and keeps Henry Hub 20% above its base level. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by a moderate 150 $/MWh on each shocked day, and the Z6 NY basis adds 3 $/MWh. Load runs 15% above a typical winter day, lifting the retail obligation P5 on every hour. Real-time on-peak prices clear 40% above day-ahead on the shocked days because the city relies on real-time balancing, which reduces the day-ahead-minus-real-time receipt in P3. The long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4 gain partly from the higher gas price, offsetting some of the loss. The scenario tests cumulative exposure over a long window at moderate intensity.

A two-day acute N.Y.C. supply failure, with no change in Henry Hub, drives the N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread up by 450 $/MWh, close to the upper edge of the winter historical range. Real-time on-peak prices clear 150% above day-ahead as the city is short in real time, which hits the day-ahead-minus-real-time receipt in P3 hard. Winter load runs 30% above a typical day as the cold peak arrives, which enlarges the short retail obligation P5 on every hour served. WEST prices are unchanged, so P1 and P4 are essentially flat and the loss sits almost entirely in the zone-volume and dart channels. This is a short, very intense shock that tests the book's concentration in P5 and P3 rather than its duration exposure.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A continental gas rally lifts Henry Hub 50% over nine days as storage drawdowns and pipeline outages tighten the national market. The Z6 NY delivered basis widens by 4 $/MWh, which raises the gas cost used by the heat-rate call P4 and lowers its payoff. Gas-fired pocket units in N.Y.C. set the city's marginal price, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread widens by 190 $/MWh on each shocked day while upstate hydro and nuclear limit the WEST move. Winter load runs 10% above a typical day, which enlarges the short retail obligation P5 on every hour it serves. WEST on-peak prices are not moved separately, so the long WEST swap P1 gains little. The loss is driven by P5 on the persistent spread, with P4 as a secondary gas-cost channel and P2 offsetting part of the spread. This is a broad gas-price shock with a sustained pocket spread, not a pure local event.

A fourteen-day gas delivery shortfall into N.Y.C. keeps the pocket spread moderately wide at 120 $/MWh on each shocked day. Because the city cannot schedule gas reliably, real-time balancing clears 70% above day-ahead on the shocked days, which reduces the day-ahead-minus-real-time receipt in P3 across its off-peak hours. Winter load runs 20% above a typical day during the cold stretch, enlarging the short retail obligation P5. Henry Hub is unchanged, so the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 are essentially flat. The loss accumulates over the full two weeks, with P5 the dominant channel, the real-time premium a secondary channel, and P2 offsetting part of the spread. This tests the combination of a long, moderate pocket spread and a real-time imbalance channel with no gas-price move.

A twelve-day N.Y.C. gas constraint widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST on-peak spread by 260 $/MWh on each shocked day, with load held at a typical winter level so the loss comes from the spread rather than from load. Henry Hub is unchanged, and the Z6 NY basis adds 6 $/MWh, which lowers the heat-rate call P4 through its gas cost. WEST on-peak prices stay near their unshocked level, so the long WEST swap P1 contributes little. The short retail obligation P5 accumulates the spread loss across the full period, partly offset by the long N.Y.C.-WEST spread P2. Real-time and day-ahead prices are assumed to move together, so P3 is not a driver. This scenario tests a long-duration, moderate-load pocket squeeze driven by a basis and spread channel rather than a spike or a national gas move.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 1,000 MW shortfall in large-load arrivals, about 3% of the 31,600 MW summer normal peak, lowers the daily peak ratio to 0.97. Day-ahead schedules were set on the forecast that included these loads, so real-time clears 84% below day-ahead on the shocked days. Upstate supply then exceeds need, pulling the WEST on-peak price down 70% beyond the load effect. N.Y.C. stays pinned by its import and locational constraints, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 20 $/MWh. This hurts P1 and P4 (long WEST), P3 (real-time below day-ahead helps P3 but the WEST move dominates P1/P4), and P5 (short N.Y.C. load against a widening spread). Duration is the full 30-day horizon.

A 1,500 MW shortfall in large-load arrivals, the near-term low end of the Gold Book shortfall range, lowers the summer peak ratio to 0.95. Because the new N.Y.C. loads are not arriving, N.Y.C. locational reserve and import needs are reshaped and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 60 $/MWh, which is inside the summer historical ceiling. The retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. load and loses heavily when this spread widens. Day-ahead is moderately above real-time, with real-time 50% below day-ahead, and WEST on-peak falls 40% beyond the load effect, which hurts P1 and P4. The shock runs for the full 30-day horizon.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

A 1,400 MW shortfall in large-load arrivals, near the 2035 Gold Book low end, lowers the summer peak ratio to 0.92 as load ramps slower than planned. The reduced load weakens upstate prices sharply, so WEST on-peak falls 80% beyond the load effect, close to the historical floor of the summer ceiling. Because N.Y.C. locational needs do not fall with the system, the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 120 $/MWh. P5 loses on its short N.Y.C. obligation and on its long WEST hedge. P1 and P4 lose from the WEST drop. Real-time runs 40% above day-ahead on the shocked days, which adds a modest P3 loss. The shock runs for 20 days, the length of the shortfall window in this scenario.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4.
